title: The Marigold Kitchen Case
subtitle: Fourteen people fell ill after Tuesday's lunch. Crack the case, and learn what compliance really means.

briefing.heading: Case briefing
paragraphs: Marigold Kitchen is a small catering company: eight staff, one walk-in fridge, and lunches for offices around town. On Tuesday 21 May it delivered forty chicken wraps to Fernway Accountants. By evening, fourteen of the people who ate them had food poisoning.

Kitchens like Marigold work under rules: food-safety **laws**, the **regulations** inspectors enforce, and the kitchen's own written **policies**. Following those rules, and being able to show honestly that you did, is called **compliance**. Everyone at Marigold says they were compliant. Someone is wrong.
The food-safety inspector arrives on Friday. Dana, the owner, has asked you to find out what really happened before then.
briefing.question: Why did fourteen people fall ill after Tuesday's chicken wraps?
briefing.stakes: Search the locations, pin what you find to the board, rule theories out with evidence, then name the explanation.

detective.title: You are the detective Dana has called in
detective.description: You don't need to know food law. You need to notice things, ask good questions, and keep asking why each clue matters.

cast.name: Dana Okafor
cast.bio: Opened Marigold six years ago. Proud of the five-star hygiene rating by the door.

cast.name: Marcus Bell
cast.bio: Fifteen years in kitchens. Runs the fridge, the rota and the logs.

cast.name: Ray Duarte
cast.bio: Made Tuesday's wraps. Has barely slept since.

cast.name: Jo Park
cast.bio: Fourteen of her team were off sick on Wednesday.

cast.name: Bo Lindqvist
cast.bio: Drives Marigold's chilled van. Keeps a van log to the minute.

cast.name: Dr Priya Nair
cast.bio: Tests food samples for the council. Explains bacteria without the jargon.

hypotheses.title: A bad batch from the supplier
hypotheses.statement: The chicken was bad when it arrived. Marigold's certificates and records are all in order, so the fault can't be in its own kitchen.
hypotheses.tempting: The paperwork really does look perfect, and blaming an outside supplier is comfortable: it means nobody inside has to change anything.
hypotheses.why: The chicken arrived at 3 °C and in date, and the same batch was fine in thirty other kitchens. And "our records are in order" turned out to mean "our records were filled in", not "our records are true". Having documents is not the same as following the rules.

hypotheses.title: One careless new cook
hypotheses.statement: Ray, barely a week into the job, broke the rules. Replace him and the problem is solved.
hypotheses.tempting: Ray made the wraps, he is new, and one person is a tidy answer: it means the rest of the kitchen is fine.
hypotheses.why: Ray was never trained as the handbook requires, the alarm was taped over before he started, the log was being faked by his manager, and he was the one person who noticed the chicken felt warm and said so. Compliance failures are usually a system failing, not one bad apple.

hypotheses.title: The rules are just red tape
hypotheses.statement: Food-safety limits are box-ticking. A fridge at 9 °C instead of 5 °C makes no real difference; this was a fluke.
hypotheses.tempting: Most days nothing bad happens when a rule is bent, so rules start to feel like paperwork for its own sake.
hypotheses.why: Dr Nair's test shows the limit sits where bacteria almost stop growing. After four days at 9 °C, chicken that looks and smells fine carries enough bacteria to make people ill. Rules exist because of real harms; "a few degrees" was the whole difference.

hypotheses.title: It went bad at the customer's office
hypotheses.statement: The food was fine when it left Marigold. Fernway Accountants must have stored it badly.
hypotheses.tempting: The last place food was seen is the easiest place to blame, and it moves the problem out of Marigold's hands.
hypotheses.why: The wraps travelled half an hour in a chilled van and were eaten at once; they never went near Fernway's fridge. There was no time and no place for things to go wrong there.

hypotheses.title: The checks happened on paper, not in the kitchen
hypotheses.statement: Marigold had the right rules, but its daily fridge checks were written up without being done, so a fridge running at 9 °C went unnoticed for weeks and spoiled good chicken.
hypotheses.why: Every piece of evidence points here. The thermostat was set to 9 °C, the alarm was taped over, the probe was never used, the log was filled in on Fridays (even for a closed Sunday), and the data logger shows the real temperature. The rules were fine. Compliance broke in the everyday routine and in the honesty of the records.

clues.title: Thermostat set to 9 °C
clues.text: The walk-in fridge's dial is set to 9 °C, with a sticky note: "Leave at 9, saves the compressor. M."
clues.proves: The fridge was run above the 5 °C limit on purpose, not by accident.
clues.why: A rule only protects people when it is actually followed. Here the rule existed, but the setting on the wall broke it every hour of every day.

clues.title: Alarm taped over
clues.text: The fridge alarm's speaker is covered in tape, marked "MUTED 02/05 - M.B."
clues.proves: The warning that would have caught a warm fridge was silenced on 2 May by Marcus, eleven days before Ray started.

rulesOut.because: The alarm was silenced before Ray's first day. The kitchen was already set up to miss a warm fridge, whoever was cooking.

clues.why: Safety rules usually come with a check that catches mistakes. Switching the check off turns a small fault into a hidden one.

clues.title: Five-star certificate
clues.text: A framed five-star food hygiene rating by the door, dated June last year.
clues.proves: Nothing about this week. It shows the kitchen passed an inspection on one day last year.
clues.why: The classic red herring of compliance: proof that you were compliant once is not proof that you are now. Compliance is a daily habit, not a frame on the wall.

clues.title: Probe never used
clues.text: The probe thermometer the handbook requires is still in its packaging, battery tab never pulled.
clues.proves: Nobody has taken a real reading with it, so the numbers in the log did not come from a measurement.
clues.why: A check needs a tool and a habit. Buying the tool looked compliant; the habit never started.

clues.title: The 5 °C rule
clues.text: Handbook 4.1: chilled food is stored at 5 °C or below, the legal limit for this kind of kitchen.
clues.proves: The law sets a limit and Marigold's own policy repeats it. The rule was known and written down.
clues.why: Most compliance works like this: a law sets the floor, and the company writes a policy so staff know what to do on an ordinary Tuesday.

clues.title: Checks twice a day
clues.text: Handbook 4.2: the person on shift probes the fridge at opening and at 2 pm, and logs the reading at the time.
clues.proves: The rule is not just "keep it cold" but "check, and write down what you actually saw".
clues.why: Records exist so a problem shows up early, and so anyone (an owner, an inspector) can see what really happened.

clues.title: Training before the first shift
clues.text: Handbook 4.4: new staff complete food-hygiene training before their first shift.
clues.proves: Training new people is Marigold's own duty, by its own rules.
clues.why: A policy is a promise the company makes to its staff and customers. Worth asking: was this one kept for Ray?

clues.title: Arrived at 3 °C
clues.text: The supplier's driver probed the chicken at 3 °C on arrival on Friday 17 May; use-by Friday 24 May.
clues.proves: The chicken was cold and in date when it reached Marigold.

rulesOut.because: The chicken arrived safe. Whatever went wrong happened after it went into Marigold's fridge.

clues.why: Good suppliers keep their own records. Here it is the supplier's honest paperwork that clears them.

clues.title: Same batch, no complaints
clues.text: The same batch of chicken went to about thirty kitchens. None reported a problem.
clues.proves: If the chicken itself had been bad, other kitchens would have seen illness too.

rulesOut.because: Thirty kitchens used the same batch without a single complaint, so the batch itself was fine.

clues.why: Comparing with others who handled the same thing is one of the fastest ways to find where the rules broke.

clues.title: Readings on a closed Sunday
clues.text: The fridge log shows two readings of 4 °C signed "M.B." on Sunday 19 May, when the kitchen was closed.
clues.proves: The log was filled in without the checks being done. It looked perfect and it wasn't true.

rulesOut.because: "Our records are in order" falls apart here: the records were in order and false. A record only proves compliance if it records what really happened.

clues.why: This is why compliance has two halves: following the rule, and being able to show it honestly. A faked record hides the very problem it was meant to catch.

clues.title: The real temperatures
clues.text: The data logger shows the walk-in fridge at 8 to 10 °C every hour since 2 May.
clues.proves: The fridge was too warm for almost three weeks while the log said 4 °C twice a day.

rulesOut.because: Good chicken then spent four days at around 9 °C in Marigold's own fridge. That alone explains it, wherever the chicken came from.

clues.why: An automatic record is hard to argue with. It is also only useful if someone looks at it.

clues.title: What 9 °C does
clues.text: In Dr Nair's test, cooked chicken kept four days at 9 °C grew enough bacteria to make people ill. At 4 °C it stayed safe.
clues.proves: A few degrees over the limit, for a few days, turns safe food into a hazard, with no change in look or smell.

rulesOut.because: The 5 °C limit is not arbitrary: it is roughly where bacteria almost stop growing. "A few degrees" is the whole difference.

clues.why: Behind almost every rule is a harm someone has measured. Knowing the reason makes a rule much easier to keep when it is inconvenient.

clues.title: Under an hour, van to desk
clues.text: The wraps left Marigold at 11:20 in a chilled van and were eaten by 12:30.
clues.proves: The food had no time to spoil after it left the kitchen.

rulesOut.because: Half an hour in a chilled van and straight onto desks leaves no room for the food to go bad at Fernway.

clues.why: Rebuilding the order of events stops you blaming the last place something was seen.

clues.title: Eaten straight away
clues.text: Jo says the lunch arrived just before twelve and was eaten at once. It never went in Fernway's fridge.
clues.proves: There was no storage step at the customer's end where things could go wrong.

rulesOut.because: The wraps were never stored at Fernway, so Fernway's fridge played no part.

clues.why: Asking the people at the other end is part of an investigation too: it closes off whole explanations quickly.

clues.title: Only the chicken wraps
clues.text: Everyone who fell ill ate the chicken wraps. Nobody who had the falafel wraps was sick.
clues.proves: The problem was the chicken, not the bread, the van or the office.
clues.why: A clue can fit more than one theory. This one narrows the search to the chicken, but on its own it can't say whether the chicken arrived bad or went bad. Only contradictions eliminate.

clues.title: Filled in on Fridays
clues.text: Marcus admits he writes up the whole week's fridge log on Friday afternoons, without taking readings.
clues.proves: The checks the handbook requires were not being done at all; only the paperwork was.

rulesOut.because: The system that should have caught a warm fridge was broken by the manager's routine, long before Ray made a single wrap.

clues.why: When records are written to look right instead of to tell the truth, compliance becomes theatre. The paperwork passes; the customers get ill.

clues.title: Never trained
clues.text: Ray never had the food-hygiene training the handbook requires before a first shift. He was told to "tick the log" if Marcus wasn't in.
clues.proves: Marigold broke its own training rule, and taught its newest cook to fake the checks.

rulesOut.because: Ray did what he was shown. It isn't one person's carelessness when the company never trained him and taught him to tick the box.

clues.why: Compliance is a system. Rules, training, checks and records hold each other up; skip the training and the newest person is set up to fail.

clues.title: Ray raised it
clues.text: On Tuesday morning Ray told Marcus the chicken felt warm. Marcus pointed at the log and told him to carry on.
clues.proves: A warning came in time, and was dismissed because the false record said all was well.

rulesOut.because: The "careless" cook was the only person who noticed. The failure was what happened when he spoke up.

clues.why: Handbook 4.5 says anyone can stop food going out. A rule like that only works if people feel safe using it, and if the record they are checked against is true.

locations.name: The kitchen
locations.summary: Where Tuesday's wraps were made. Look closely at everything.
locations.intro: Stainless steel, a humming walk-in fridge, a radio playing to nobody. Tap or select anything that catches your eye.

hotspots.label: Walk-in fridge
hotspots.note: Cool inside, but not cold. Your breath doesn't fog. Raw vegetables, sauces and a half-used tray of cooked chicken.

hotspots.label: Fridge thermostat
hotspots.note: The dial points at 9 °C. A sticky note reads: "Leave at 9, saves the compressor. M."

hotspots.label: Fridge alarm
hotspots.note: The alarm's speaker is wrapped in grey tape. Written on it in marker: "MUTED 02/05 - M.B."

hotspots.label: Hygiene certificate
hotspots.note: A framed five-star food hygiene rating, dated June last year. Dana straightens it every morning.

hotspots.label: Hand-wash sink
hotspots.note: Soap, hot water, paper towels. Exactly as it should be.

hotspots.label: Utensil drawer
hotspots.note: Under the ladles: the probe thermometer the handbook mentions, still sealed in its packaging.

hotspots.label: Waste bin
hotspots.note: Eggshells and vegetable peelings. Eggs weren't in Tuesday's wraps. Nothing to see here.

locations.name: The staff handbook
locations.summary: Marigold's own written rules on food safety, signed off by Dana.
locations.intro: Every member of staff signs to say they have read this. Read it as a detective: which lines matter to what happened?
locations.prompt: Highlight the lines that matter to this case.

lines.text: 4.1 Chilled food is stored at 5 °C or below. This is the legal limit for a kitchen like ours.
4.2 The person on shift probes the walk-in fridge at opening and at 2 pm, and writes the reading in the fridge log at the time.
4.3 Fridge alarms are never switched off. A fault is reported to Dana the same day.
lines.note: Hold on to this one. Have you looked at the alarm in the kitchen?

lines.text: 4.4 New staff complete food-hygiene training before their first shift.
4.5 Anyone who spots a food-safety problem can stop food going out. Nobody is blamed for raising a concern.
lines.note: A good rule. Whether people feel safe using it is another question.

lines.text: 4.6 Staff wear clean aprons and tie back long hair.
lines.note: True, and followed. Not part of this case.

lines.text: 4.7 Allergen information is kept with every product label.
lines.note: Important, but nobody here has an allergic reaction.

locations.name: Goods-in records
locations.summary: The supplier's delivery note next to Marigold's own goods-in sheet.
locations.intro: Two records of the same delivery: Friday's chicken. They should agree.
locations.prompt: Compare the two exhibits row by row. Select any row that matters.

left.label: Exhibit A: supplier's delivery note
left.caption: Fresh Fields Poultry, signed by their driver

right.label: Exhibit B: Marigold goods-in sheet
right.caption: Filled in by whoever receives the delivery

spots.note: The supplier probed the chicken at 3 °C, inside the 5 °C limit. Marigold's own sheet leaves the box empty.
Nobody at Marigold signed for the delivery. Their own goods-in check was skipped, though the supplier's reading still covers the chicken.

locations.sameNote: These two agree. Nothing hiding in this row.

locations.name: The fridge log
locations.summary: The clipboard hanging on the fridge door. Dana reads it every Friday.
locations.intro: Dana calls this log "perfect". Check it against the rule and against what you know about the week.
locations.prompt: Find the row that cannot be true.
locations.rule: Handbook 4.2: probe at opening and at 2 pm, logged at the time by the person on shift. Limit 5 °C. The kitchen is closed on Sundays.

mismatches.note: The kitchen was closed on Sunday, yet two readings are signed. Nobody was there to take them.

locations.okNote: On its own this row looks fine. That is the trouble with a log: it only shows what someone wrote.

locations.name: Fridge data logger
locations.summary: A small locked box on the fridge wall that records the real temperature every hour.
locations.intro: Dana had forgotten it existed. Marcus set its code the day he "sorted out the alarm".
locations.lockedNote: You have no reason to look at the fridge wall yet. Search the kitchen first.
locations.prompt: The box has a four-digit combination lock. Turn the dials and try the code.
hints: Marcus set the code on the day he dealt with the alarm.
The tape on the fridge alarm has a date on it, written day then month.
locations.openText: The lid clicks open. The logger's little screen scrolls through three weeks of hourly readings.

locations.name: Council food lab
locations.summary: Dr Priya Nair can show you what temperature does to cooked chicken.
locations.intro: "Pick a temperature and a time, and I'll run it on a sample of cooked chicken. The numbers are rounded, but the pattern is real."
locations.prompt: Set the storage conditions, then run the test.

outcomes.text: At 4 °C bacteria barely grow. That is exactly why the limit sits where it does.
A day in a properly cold fridge changes almost nothing.
Even after four days at 4 °C the chicken is safe, and well inside its use-by date.
A few degrees too warm and the bacteria wake up. After six hours you couldn't see or smell any difference.
After a day at 9 °C the count has climbed about a hundredfold. It still looks and smells fine.
Four days at 9 °C, as long as Tuesday's chicken sat in Marigold's fridge. It looks normal, and it would make people ill.

locations.name: Tuesday's timeline
locations.summary: Bo's van log and the delivery paperwork. Put the events in order.
locations.intro: "Half these food rules are just forms, if you ask me. But my van log is spot on, and the van's chilled. Here's everything I've got."
locations.prompt: Put the events in the order they happened. The times are hidden until you get it.

events.text: The chicken arrives from the supplier and goes into the walk-in fridge.
Ray makes forty chicken wraps from it.
Bo loads the wraps into the chilled van.
The wraps arrive at Fernway Accountants.
Fernway staff eat lunch at their desks.
The first people report stomach cramps.

locations.solvedNote: From the van to the first bite was well under an hour, all of it chilled. But the chicken sat in Marigold's fridge for four days. Whatever happened, happened in the kitchen.

locations.name: Interview: Dana
locations.summary: The owner. Worried, proud, and sure the problem came from outside.
locations.opening: "Thank you for coming. The inspector is here on Friday and I need to know what happened. We're a good kitchen. We've got the certificates to prove it."

questions.ask: Would you say Marigold is compliant?
questions.answer: "Completely. Five-star hygiene rating, every certificate on the wall, the handbook signed by everyone. If an inspector asks for paperwork, we have it."

questions.ask: Who makes sure the rules are actually followed day to day?
questions.answer: "Marcus runs the kitchen. I read the fridge log every Friday and it's always perfect. Always 4 degrees."

questions.ask: Where does the chicken come from?
questions.answer: "Fresh Fields Poultry. They supply half the cafés in town. I'd put money on a bad batch."

questions.ask: Have other Fresh Fields customers had problems?
questions.answer: "I rang round this morning. The same batch went to about thirty kitchens and... no. Not a single complaint."

questions.ask: Have you seen what people are saying online?
questions.answer: "Someone posted that "the new kid poisoned everyone". Ray's been in pieces since."
questions.note: An online rumour is not evidence. It names a person, which feels like an explanation, but it is a guess repeated loudly.

locations.name: Interview: Marcus
locations.summary: The kitchen manager. Defensive, experienced, and quick to name the new cook.
locations.opening: "Look, I've run kitchens for fifteen years. Nobody got sick on my watch until the new lad started."

questions.ask: Why do you think it was Ray?
questions.answer: "He made the wraps, didn't he? Someone careless did something careless."
questions.note: Ray did make the wraps, but who touched the food last is not the same as what made it unsafe. Blaming the newest person stops an investigation too early.

questions.ask: Why is the fridge set to 9 °C?
questions.answer: "The compressor kept icing up and the power bill was through the roof. Five degrees is over the top anyway. Those limits are written by people who've never worked a kitchen."

questions.ask: Who taped over the fridge alarm?
questions.answer: "It kept beeping, all day, every day. I taped it at the start of May. It was driving everyone mad."

questions.ask: Who signed the fridge log on Sunday, when the kitchen was closed?
questions.answer: "...Fine. I write the log up on Friday afternoons for the whole week. The fridge is always fine, so what's the difference?"

questions.ask: Did Ray get his food-hygiene training before his first shift?
questions.answer: "We were short-staffed. I showed him where things are. His training is booked for next month."

locations.name: Interview: Ray
locations.summary: The new cook who made the wraps. Everyone is looking at him.
locations.opening: "I made the wraps. I keep going over it. I did everything Marcus showed me."

questions.ask: Did anything seem wrong on Tuesday morning?
questions.answer: "The chicken didn't feel fridge-cold. More like... cool. I said so to Marcus."
"He said the log says 4 degrees, so it's fine, and to get the wraps out. It was my second week. I didn't want to make trouble."

questions.ask: Did anyone train you in food safety?
questions.answer: "Not really. I was told to tick the log if Marcus wasn't in. Nobody showed me the probe thermometer."

questions.ask: Have you read the staff handbook?
questions.answer: "I signed to say I had. It was in a pile of about forty forms on my first day."

locations.name: Interview: Jo
locations.summary: The customer. She wants to know it won't happen again.
locations.opening: "Fourteen of my team were off sick on Wednesday. I'm not after anyone's head. I just want to know it won't happen again."

questions.ask: When did the lunch arrive, and when was it eaten?
questions.answer: "Just before twelve. We ate at our desks straight away. It never went near our office fridge."
"Only people who had the chicken wraps. Everyone who had the falafel ones was fine."

questions.ask: Have you heard anything about the cause?
questions.answer: "Someone in the office said Marigold's van has no fridge in it. I don't know if that's true."
questions.note: Bo's van is chilled, and the delivery took half an hour. A rumour about the van is easy to repeat and easy to check, and it doesn't survive the timeline.

board.heading: The case board
board.intro: Pin clues, then link each one to a theory it speaks to. Evidence that contradicts a theory rules it out. Evidence that fits is not proof.

accusation.intro: Pick the theory the evidence leaves standing, and say how sure you are. Nothing is scored: the debrief explains every theory either way.

epilogue.heading: Epilogue
paragraphs: **Compliance** means following the rules that apply to your work (laws, regulations, standards and your organisation's own policies) and being able to show, honestly, that you did.
Rules exist because of real harms. The 5 °C limit is where bacteria nearly stop growing. The alarm, the probe and the log are there so a warm fridge is noticed on day one, not in week three.

Day to day, compliance looks small: a reading taken and written down truthfully, a new starter trained before their first shift, an alarm left on, a concern raised and acted on. A certificate on the wall shows you passed once. Compliance is the habit that keeps you passing.
takeaways: Compliance is following the rules that apply to you, and being able to show it honestly.
Paperwork is not compliance. A record only counts if it records what really happened.
Every rule protects someone from a real harm; knowing the reason makes it easier to keep.
It's a system: rules, training, checks and records hold each other up.
When something goes wrong, look at the system before blaming the newest person.
Anyone should be able to raise a concern, and it should be acted on.
